newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand catches a chill, in need of good medicine.
newsitem.headline: Thailand catches a chill, in need of good medicine.

text.p: Once-robust Thailand, suffering from unprecedented economic malaise and a severe image problem, is in dire need of a good cure, economic analysts said on Thursday.

Export growth this year has fallen, the economy is slowing, the stock market has plummeted to three-year-lows, the current account deficit is ballooning and political uncertainties surround the November 17 general election, they told Reuters.
For a nation that has enjoyed an average annual economic growth rate of nine percent over the past decade, the current state of affairs is a bitter pill to swallow.
Foreign investors have fled the stock market in droves, underweighting Thai stocks in favour of equities in other booming Asian countries.

Banks have been hit by restrictive central bank borrowing policies. Interest rates are set to stay high despite earlier expectations of some easing and foreign lenders are thinking twice about lending to Thai borrowers, analysts said.
"The Thai economy is sick. There is no quick fix. What is needed is strong, bitter medicine in the form of new drastic measures," said Susheel Narula, head of research at Seamico Securities.

Media allegations this year that the government and its economic ministers had mismanaged the economy added to insinuations of corruption all combined to project a negative image of the country abroad, analysts said.
"Whether exaggerated or real, all this has led to a loss of confidence in Thailand," said a Merrill Lynch analyst.
To restore faith in the country, it was vital that the new government that will replace the out-going Banharn Silpa-archa administration should be widely acceptable, analysts said.
Several major research houses have cut growth forecasts for Thailand's 1996 economy to below 7.0 percent from a high 8.6 last year.

"For any other country, economic growth of around seven percent would be great news. But for Thailand, which has been used to very high growth for a long time, it is bad news," said Pisarn Manoleehagul, head of Thai Farmers' Research Centre.
"You can write the rest of this year off and probably even early next year for any sort of real recovery," he added.
Export growth, and profitability in the traditionally strong banking sector, are both seen down this year to single figures from last year's double figures, analysts said.
They said investors question banks' asset quality, believing that problem loans especially to the weak property sector may be more than expected with profits hit by high lending rates.
The minimum lending rate is around 13.75 percent and banks are set to raise fixed deposit rates by at least 25 basis points soon.
The Bank of Thailand recently moved to restrict foreign loans imports by local and foreign banks through their offshore units to curb any serious rise in the country's short-term foreign debt.
Short-term foreign debt jumped to $41.1 billion, or half of Thailand's total external debt at end-1995, from $15.4 billion at end-1991.
"The central bank move is a prudent one that would make banks face up to realities," said a Singapore analyst who declined to be identified.
With limited avenues for bringing in short-term foreign capital into the country the race has begun among banks to mobilise capital from tight domestic funds.
